#### [Publication](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/publications)

#### June 1, 2026

#### [Auf Deutsch lesen](https://algorithmwatch.org/de/ki-klimaschwindel/)

#### [#sustainability](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/hashtag/sustainability/)

In a very short time, a new environmentally harmful industry has emerged. The rapid proliferation of data centers—driven by technologies marketed as “artificial intelligence” (AI)—has become a promising prospect for the fossil fuel industry. This harmful trend is justified by the claim that “AI” will ultimately make up for these shortcomings by delivering a net benefit for climate protection. This report by Ketan Joshi and civil society partners examines for the first time whether such claims stand up to scrutiny by identifying the different types of AI to which the claims refer and evaluating the validity of the cited evidence. The report concludes that the climate impacts of energy-intensive generative AI are deliberately obscured and downplayed by generalized “AI sustainability claims,” which lump entirely different technologies together and equate harmful generative AI with older, "traditional" AI. Furthermore, this report shows that the majority of AI climate promises rely on remarkably weak evidence, and in some cases, no evidence at all. This constitutes a new form of greenwashing by the tech industry that must be urgently countered.

## **Key findings: Bait-and-switch and weak evidence**

This analysis collected the most prominent AI climate claims and determined a) what types of AI were referred to and b) what evidence was presented to back up those claims. It finds that:

- Most claims of climate benefit relate to "traditional" AI, which has a much lower environmental impact than consumer generative AI tools. Even if these benefits are real, they are unrelated to - and dwarfed by - the massive expansion of energy use from the generative AI industry.
- Where claims of traditional AI climate benefits are made, they tend to rely on weaker forms of evidence, such as corporate websites, rather than published academic research. Only 26% cited published academic research, while 36% did not cite any evidence at all.

The tech companies driving AI expansion claim that AI will eventually help solve climate change. Our analysis indicates that such claims are not based on credible and verifiable data. On the contrary, the evidence for any significant positive climate impacts from AI is weak, while its substantial climate damage is clearly documented.
